young.html: About 2,500 years ago, a man named Herodotus set out to answer a big question: why did the Greeks and the Persians go to war? To find out, he traveled and asked questions everywhere he went, in Egypt, around the Black Sea, in the cities of Greece and Asia Minor. Then he wrote it all down. His book is the oldest great history we have, and the Greek word he used for it, historiē, meant "inquiry", finding out by asking. That is where our word history comes from.

The Persian Empire was the biggest the world had seen. Its kings, Darius and then his son Xerxes, sent huge armies against the Greeks, who lived in many small, quarrelsome cities. Against the odds, the Greeks won: at Marathon in 490 BC, and ten years later in the sea battle of Salamis. Before Salamis, a small band of Spartans and their allies held the narrow pass of Thermopylae for three days.

young.html: Herodotus loved a good story, and he put them all in: a clever thief who outwits the king of Egypt, a musician rescued by a dolphin, ants as big as foxes that dig for gold. Sometimes he says plainly that he doesn't believe a story he was told, but he writes it down anyway, so his readers can judge.

Be a historian. Choose an event from before you were born: how your grandparents met, the day your town got its library, a family move. Ask two or three people who remember it. Do their stories match? Write down what they agree on, and where they differ. That is what Herodotus did.

full.html: Herodotus (c. 484–c. 425 BC) was born in Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum, in Turkey), a Greek city then under Persian rule. He traveled widely and later joined the new Athenian-led colony of Thurii in southern Italy. The Roman writer Cicero called him "the father of history". His work, written in the Ionic dialect of Greek, was later divided into nine books, each named for one of the nine Muses.

full.text: This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another.
full.author: Herodotus
full.note: Hellenes: Greeks. To the Greeks, "barbarians" meant anyone who didn't speak Greek, not "savages".

full.html: He set out to do two things at once: to keep great deeds from being forgotten, and to explain causes. That second aim is what makes him a historian and not only a storyteller.

full.cap: The invasions of 490 and 480 BC. Step through the campaign; each step notes the book of the Histories that tells it.

full.html: Book I tells how Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, asked the Athenian lawgiver Solon who was the happiest man in the world, expecting to hear his own name. Solon named ordinary people who had lived and died well, and warned:

full.text: … before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate.
full.author: Herodotus

full.html: Croesus later lost his kingdom to Cyrus of Persia. (The dates suggest the two men could hardly have met; Herodotus tells the story for its lesson.) Sophocles' Oedipus ends with the same thought.

In 480 BC Xerxes led his army into Greece. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, King Leonidas of Sparta, with his 300 Spartans and several thousand allies, held them for three days, until a local man named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas sent most of the allies away and stayed to fight. Herodotus records a Spartan's answer to the news that Persian arrows would hide the sun:

full.text: … the Spartan Dienekes is said to have proved himself the best man of all, the same who, as they report, uttered this saying before they engaged battle with the Medes … he said that their guest from Trachis brought them very good news, for if the Medes obscured the light of the sun, the battle against them would be in the shade and not in the sun.
full.author: Herodotus
full.note: Shortened where marked. The Medes: Herodotus' name for the Persians and their allies.

full.html: Freedom and law. For Herodotus, the war was a contest between a great empire ruled by one man and small cities governed by their own laws. In one scene the exiled Spartan king Demaratus tells Xerxes that the Spartans are free, but not wholly free, because they fear their law more than Xerxes' subjects fear him.

Herodotus treats the Persians, Egyptians and Scythians with real curiosity. He says that if all people were asked to choose the best customs, each would choose their own, and he takes that as a reason for respect, not contempt.

Thinking Herodotus believed every story he told. He often says "the Persians say", "the Egyptians say", or "this I do not believe", and he sometimes gives two or three versions. He reports; the reader is meant to weigh.

deep.html: Thucydides, on the next rung, seems to have Herodotus in mind when he complains about history written to please listeners. Plutarch, centuries later, wrote a whole essay, "On the Malice of Herodotus", accusing him of bias. Modern archaeology has confirmed much of what he reports, for example about Egypt and the Scythians, and shown other parts to be wrong or legendary. Historians today treat him as an invaluable source who must be read with care, which is what he asked for.

items: Is a history better if it leaves out the stories it can't prove, or if it includes them with a warning?
Herodotus says each people thinks its own customs best. Is that a reason to respect other customs, or to doubt all of them?
Why might small cities have beaten a vast empire?
Can we ever know the true cause of a war?

deep.html: Thucydides set a stricter standard; Plutarch's Lives retell many of the same people, Themistocles, Aristides and others, on the Rome rungs. Herodotus' account of Egypt is still read on the site's Egyptology Ladder.

questions: Herodotus asked many people the same question and wrote down all their answers. Why is it useful to hear more than one side?
Which of Herodotus' stories would you most like to be true?
The Spartans at Thermopylae stayed when they could have left. What do you think of their choice?
Solon says no one should be called happy until the end of life. Do you agree?
If someone wrote the history of your family, what would you want them to be sure to get right?
care: The Histories describe battles and some cruel customs and punishments, in a matter-of-fact way. This lesson keeps to the main story. Young readers enjoy Book II (Egypt) and the tales in Book I, read aloud with a parent choosing the passages.
